utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Judge Van den Wyngaert is not able to sit this morning. We do anticipate she will be sitting again on Monday, and Judge Thelin and I will continue the hearing this morning under the Rule. Could I mention for Mr. Saxon and other counsel, and particularly for the witness, that to ease the time problem today and to try and ensure that we can finish the professor's evidence, we will sit for three full one and a half hour sessions and have a one-hour break at 12.30, resuming at 1.30 through to 3.00. So if it is possible, Mr. Saxon, for you to have that in mind; and, hopefully, it will prove possible for you to finish your cross-examination and Ms. Residovic to conclude her re-examination in that extended time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I remind you, Professor, the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies. Now Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution's first binder be given back to the witness, please, so that she can see her expert report. And if we could turn to the witness's report, which I believe is now 1D00309. I believe the court officer is ahead of me on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Professor, if you could turn to paragraph 55, please, of your report. Paragraph 55, in the first sentence, says that: "With a view to determine what duties and obligations each category of authorised officials has under the Law of Macedonia, it is therefore necessary to read the Law on Internal Affairs together with any particular legal provision that specifies the role and responsibilities of the category of authorised officials that is under consideration." Then, as authority, in footnote 47, you cite to Article 47 of the Law on Organisation and Work of Government Bodies, which is Exhibit P92.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could turn to Exhibit P92, please, and if we could turn to the next page, please, in each language. Okay. I see I have the wrong document that I -- I believe the document that I need to show - I apologise - is Exhibit P95, which is at tab 53 of the first Prosecution binder. I'm told now that there is no English translation in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Nor is the document on the screen, the one you're after.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We're looking for P95.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you mean Exhibit 1D310, by any chance, Mr. Saxon? Do you want the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I'm confusing the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You don't want the number I gave you then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No. P95, which should be at tab 53 of your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could turn to that, Ms. Taseva.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I wouldn't like to add to the confusion. But for -- to make it clear for us, so that we can follow, the Prosecutor says, in line 2:13, the conclusion of the witness, footnote 47, which reads -- which quotes to Article 47 of the Law on Organisation. We see here that, in footnote 47, the transcript is cited to only. So maybe our learned colleague could clarify this a bit for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I stand corrected. I'm grateful to Ms. Residovic for correcting me. She is absolutely right that the authority cited by Professor Taseva is a portion of the transcript. That's absolutely right. Thank you for that. I apologise for the confusion. Having said that, now I would look at what is Exhibit P53. It's a decree on the use of means of coercion and fire-arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you could turn, please, to Article 7, Professor Taseva. Do you have Article 7 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise, if I misspoke again. I'm referring to P95. It's at tab 53, the first binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you have Article 7 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering the fact that I noticed many problems with the translation of documents yesterday, I would kindly ask that I receive simultaneously also the version in Macedonian language, so that I'm able to answer your questions correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You should have a copy in the Macedonian language there, underneath that green sheet in front of you, Professor. You can also see --

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- it on the screen. So you've got it twice. All right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Article 7, this particular document, the decree on the use of means of coercion and fire-arms, describes how use of force, including the use of fire-arms, can be used by authorised persons in the Ministry of Internal Affairs. And Article 7 tells us that authorised persons of the ministry acquire advanced training on the use of the means of coercion and fire-arms in the manner prescribed by special provisions. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And Article 9 -- excuse me, Article 8, an authorised person will use means of coercion against members of the army of the Republic of Macedonia in uniform only -- in uniform, only if there is no possibility to provide intervention of the police of the army of the Republic of Macedonia. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, these Articles - Article 7, Article 8 - they don't refer to specific categories of authorised officials, do they?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These provisions do not refer to a specific category or specific categories of authorised officials, that's right. These are general provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Right. These Articles refer to authorised officials in general terms, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, when authorised officials are referred to in the laws and regulations of the Ministry of Interior, they are not always precisely defined by particular categories. Sometimes we see the term "authorised officials" simply used in a broad, general term, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the acts of the Ministry of Interior, the categories of authorised officials are precisely established, and the authorisations that each of the authorised officials have and can use are precisely established in the act on systemization and organisation of the job posts within the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But, for example, with respect to the use of force, these two Articles would suggest that any authorised person can receive training in the use of fire-arms, and they would seem to suggest that any authorised persons may use force against members of -- against uniformed members of the army only in a particular situation, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This provision, which we are reviewing now, was passed by the president of the Republic of Macedonia, Mr. Branko Crvenkovski, and it is not a regulation or a document that was passed within the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Right. But you didn't answer my question. Can you answer my question, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decree that is passed by the president is a general document, which just indicates the authorised officials without further specifying who among the authorised officials have what type of authorisations and can use what type of authorisations. That is further defined in the acts of the Ministry of Interior, depending on the job posts and the duties entailed in those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could we turn, please, to Article 17 of this decree on the use of force. You will see that, just above Article 17, it's a new chapter, Chapter 3, Use of Other Means of Coercion. Article 17 says: "During carrying out of duties and tasks, the authorised persons may use chemical and gas substances," tear gas, "for restoring law and order after violation of larger scale (violent demonstrations, mass fights), removing persons from facilities, means of transportation or other areas by force." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What does the term "other areas" mean?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other premises could be any other public location.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could be any other public location. All right. Could it include a shopping mall, for instance?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could be under facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And a shopping mall is a facility?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Facilities or "objekti" in the Macedonian meaning of this word would mean any building. This is a general or generic term about any building without specifying its nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see. All right. Well, this term "other areas," could it include a football field?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It can also comprise a football field.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since another area is everything that an area denotes, a public lotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, where is that located in the law?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the law, or the decree actually, has left here room without restrictions, since public law and order could be disrupted to a larger extent also in a park. It could be disrupted at a football field. It could be disrupted also at a horse race grounds and anything else that is public space.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How about a children's playground?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You think they might be using tear gas in a children's playground?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is a need, the measures foreseen will be used whenever it is needed, according to the assessment made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Well, I think what you're telling me and what you've told us is that laws sometimes, a law like this one, leaves some room for interpretation and flexibility, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decrees, the acts of this type, have left sufficient room to make the assessment in accordance with the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the same would be true, wouldn't it, for laws that apply to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, like the Law on Internal Affairs, wouldn't it? They leave room for assessment, depending on what's going on, on the ground?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You couldn't say so. You couldn't use a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Really? Why not?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since there are numerous by-laws that are derived in a way from the Law on Internal Affairs which regulate the competencies and the way in which those competencies are implemented in detail. And the application of special authorisations is regulated by other by-laws of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the reasons those by-laws are necessary, isn't it, Professor, it's because there's a lot of room for assessment and interpretation in the Law on Internal Affairs, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our legal system, whenever a law is adopted, by-laws are necessary for the law to become applicable and implementable. Just for the sake of illustration, I will mention that for the Law on Police to become enforceable, that law was passed last year, the Ministry of Interior is presently developing more than 200 by-laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So I can take your response, then, to my question as a "yes," right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Since my explanation was my attempt to explain the legal system which operates in the way, that all details related to application of certain legal provisions are regulate the through by-laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that's --

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this does not leave room for the laws to be interpreted broadly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, if the law is so clearly written -- let's refer to the Law on Internal Affairs. If that law is so clearly and precisely written, then why is it necessary to have by-laws?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since it is necessary to establish the specific way of conduct when applying each of the action or measure or authorisation that is incorporated in the law itself. Since the law does not specify in detail the way in which it will be applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Precisely. And it's the minister of internal affairs who approves the by-laws. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If, pursuant to the law, and not only pursuant to the Law on Interior but also other legislation --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I think this is a yes-or-no question. Now we need to move along today. We're trying to move along fairly quickly so that you can go own to your other affairs. It's the minister of internal affairs who approves the by-laws that are passed, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment, we see a decree passed by the president. This is why I stated, not always such instruments are passed by the minister of the interior. Whenever authorised by the law, the minister of the interior does that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. So frequently, the minister of the interior approves the by-laws for the Ministry of Internal Affairs, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where he is authorised for that by-law, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Professor Taseva, before you left the Ministry of Internal Affairs in 2000, did you meet a colleague named Valentina Naumova who worked in the department for legal and personnel matters?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, a person who works in the department for legal and personnel matters is not considered to be an operative worker, is she?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you an answer to this question, whether she should not be considered an operative worker, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So your answer is -- so the answer to my question is "yes," I believe?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show what the witness what is Exhibit 1D113, and this is not in your binders. We have this only in e-court at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see, Professor, this is a resolution dated 18th June 2001, the Ministry of Interior, to form a commission to investigate the validity of the reports by ethnic Albanian nationals in the Republic of Macedonia that members of the Ministry of Interior violated their authority. Then we see, in Roman numeral I, that a commission is to be formed to investigates the validity of these reports composed of the following members, and you see that the fourth member is Valentina Naumova, senior advisor for legal property matters and representation in the sector for legal and personnel matters. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then, in Roman numeral II, we see that the commission is assigned the task of determining the validity of the allegations contained in the reports, both individual and group, which were submitted to the Ministry of Interior by ethnic Albanian citizens of the Republic of Macedonia, as well as by non-governmental organisations, claiming that certain members of the ministry violated their authority during the completion of their work. Have you been following with me?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor, the work of this commission to investigate whether these allegations are valid, that would involve some operative work, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The work of this committee is not operative work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, how else will the commission do its investigation?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I have displayed on the screen the first part of this document in Macedonian language, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we go to the top of the page, or the page before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Macedonian text, it reads, "Examine," which is very different from investigation. So this committee does not have a role to play in operative investigations or any other investigations that would be considered actions within the preliminary procedure. This is purely administrative procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Take a like, though, at Roman numeral II, which says that the commission is assigned the task of determining the validity of the allegations contained in the reports. Now, to make that determination, Professor, don't people have to do some investigative work?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said, this is a completely administrative procedure. We have here petitions lodged by citizens, and this committee has the task to assess whether there is any ground to forward this for further processing. If you allow me, as an illustration, I will indicate that such type of procedures are run all the time in the state anti-corruption committee which does not have investigating powers; and, also, many such petitions are filed with the non-governmental sector which does these same things, although it does not have authority to run any investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Doesn't this committee, or this commission, to do its job, need to gather whatever evidence might exist regarding allegations of criminal activity?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They have to look into what is at hand. If they can obtain any other additional information, so as to propose further procedures and undertaking further procedures, this committee comprising of persons from a number of sectors will have to validly assess whether further procedures are to be undertaken in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor Taseva, pursuant to the code of criminal procedure, and I think it's Articles 140 and 142, and I'm sure other Articles as well, police officers, operative members of the Ministry of Interior who are informed that a crime might have been committed or see a crime, an ex officio crime, they're supposed to try to gather some more information, aren't they, to see if there's -- to see if there's any grounds, to see if there's reasonable suspicion that a crime occurred, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a competency of the Ministry of Interior, but this committee is not a body which has such a competency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, the problem, Professor, that I see or the inconsistencies you told us, about a minute ago, lines 9 to 10, page 12, that this committee has the task to assess whether there is any ground to forward this for further processing. What's the difference between that task and the task of a police officer?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we have petitions by civilians who and which pertain to the work of members of the Ministry of Interior. These petitions can be of various nature. They can pertain to unseeming behaviour of a police officer. This need not be any other kind of incident. Perhaps the citizen is not pleased with the way the police officer addressed him. Perhaps he is not pleased with how this police officer is carrying out other parts of his work. We can't immediately say that there is an event which has to be observed from the point of view of a criminal procedural law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I understand that professor, but you didn't really answer my question. You told us before that the people in this commission have to assess the information to see whether there is any ground to forward this information on for further processing. Well, what's the difference between that work and the work of a police officer who also has to determine whether there are reasonable grounds that a crime has occurred and then submits a report to the public prosecutor? What's the difference?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a preliminary phase within the ministry. As I said, this is about members of the ministry, and there's the possibility of any kind of petitions. Perhaps someone will file a petition, and there have been such petitions, that they've lended 10.000 dinars to a police officer, which this police officer has not returned. In cases such as these, first, it has to be clarified what is at hand in order to see what needs to be taken further. This does not mean that it will not be necessary to proceed further. But, first, it needs to be clarified how and what needs to be undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we can turn back to the first page in the Macedonian version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor, Valentina Naumova, at the time this commission was set up, she was an advisor for legal property matters within the sector for legal and personnel matters. Evaluating these kinds of petitions, that wasn't within the remit of her job duties, was it?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evaluating these kinds of petitions falls within the remit of the sector of legal and personnel affairs because there may be various types of questions that are considered and require broader knowledge of family law, commercial law; for example, there's a petition where a wife complains of the husband not paying alimony. Does the persons who are in these sectors can help fully elucidate cases such as these, and this is the reason why commissions of this kind are established.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. I'd lake to move on to another topic, please. I'd like to talk to you about the duties and obligations of the minister of internal affairs, himself, or, in the case of the present, herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please turn to Exhibit P92, please, which will be available in e-court. This is the Law on the Organisation and Work of Government Bodies. If we could move to Article 49, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in Article 49 of this -- of this law, in the first paragraph, we see: "The minister represents the ministry, and he organises and secures the lawful and efficient completion of work and tasks ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And there are a number of other -- well, there are several other responsibilities listed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And there's a subchapter 5 called Acts of Government Bodies, and Article 55 talks about the minister, where the minister "submits rules, orders, guidelines, plans, programmes, decisions, and other types of acts for the execution of laws and other regulations, when he is authorised to do so by law." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then in Article 56, if we could go one more page in the Macedonian version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In subparagraph (2) of Article 56, we see that it says: "Orders, instruct or prohibit proceedings in a specific situation which has significance for the execution of the laws and regulations." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that subparagraph 2, that's within the remit of the minister's authority, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This Article, paragraph (1) establishes also that the rules determined further the laws and other acts in order for them to be rendered operational. This is what we spoke about previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And, Professor, that's quite a bit of authority, isn't it, what is laid out there in Article 56, subparagraph (2)?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our legislators felt that the ministers in the government of the Republic of Macedonia should have these authorisations which the legislature has awarded to them; therefore, these pertain to all ministers in the government of the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn now, please, to what is Exhibit P00551.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And by the way, can I take your last response to my question as a "yes."

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The ministers have these legal authorisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, Article 51 -- excuse me, Exhibit P551, again, is the Law on the Government of the Republic of Macedonia. This is from July 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to what is Article 13, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see, Professor, Article 13 of this law says that: "A minister manages independently the ministry to which he/she is elected, monitors and is responsible for the implementation of the laws and other regulations." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, for example, with respect to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, this particular legal provision provides for a great deal of responsibility and a great deal of authority for the minister, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct. The authorities are also established in other laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And so, for example, there's no provision here that says, for example, the president manages ministries, because that would not fall within the work of the president. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a Law on Government and does not pertain to the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's right. And there's no law that says a president can manage a ministry, is there?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no such law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to what is Exhibit P00086, which will again appear on e-court. It should be the Law on Internal Affairs. It is. And if we could turn to Article 10, please, and if we could scroll down a little bit in the English version. Could we go to Article 10, please, in the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You'll see, Professor, that Article 10 contains two paragraphs. The first paragraph says: "The policemen could accomplish the activities mentioned in Article 8 of this law in civilian clothes, as well as if the immediate supervisor or the employee authorised by him is ordering this." But it's the second paragraph that I'm more interested in. It says this: "When the public peace and order are deranged in a larger scale, the minister can order also other authorised officials from Article 24, paragraph 2, of this law, to conduct certain activities in uniform." Have you been following with me?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we agree that this provision in the Law on Internal Affairs also provides some broad powers to the minister, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister here is not mentioned anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, maybe there is a problem with the translation. Please correct me. As I read the second paragraph, it says: "When the public peace and order are deranged in a larger scale, the minister can order also other authorised officials from Article 24, paragraph 2, of this law, to conduct certain activities in uniform."

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the translation is right. Can we look at Article 24, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let's go to Article 24, if we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see that Article 24 defines who authorised officials are: Police and operative employees, and that's a lot of employees as we discussed yesterday; employees who accomplish activities that are in direct connection to police and operative activities; and the minister, his deputy, and supervisors of certain organisational units. Anyway, going back to my question related to Article 10, that second part of Article 10 grants the minister some broad powers, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are powers of the minister to order or to ask other authorised officials to act in uniform but under conditions which are specified in Article 8; only under those conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn back to Article 10, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There's no reference in Article 10 to Article 8. Article 10 says: "The minister can order other authorised officials to conduct certain activities in uniform when the public peace and order are deranged." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 1 of Article 10 points to Article 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we go up and see Article 8, please, in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see, yes: "Activities in the direct maintaining of the public peace and order, the regulation and control of the traffic on roads, control of crossings over the border, security on the lakes are carried out by the police," right, "and they should be uniformed." That's what Article 8 says?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, how does Article 8 in any way limit the powers given to the minister in the second half of Article 10?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By saying that this can happen only in cases of maintaining public law and order, regulating traffic and roads, control of state borders, and security of lakes. Only what is listed in Article 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The problem with that interpretation, Professor, is that the second part of Article 10 clearly says: "When the public peace and order are deranged on a large scale, the minister can order that certain activities be carried out by authorised officials." Right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the case when the public peace and order is under threat of a broader scale. Here it is even more narrowly stated as public peace and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor, can we agree that during the crisis time in 2001 the public peace and order in Macedonia was deranged on a large scale? Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because this was not a disruption of the public peace and order. It would be well perhaps to look at the definitions of peace and order, public peace and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I think I'm just going to move on after that, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness what is Exhibit 1D107, which should be the rule book of operations for the Ministry of Internal Affairs. And if we can turn, please, to Article 25 which will be on the 20th page in e-court in English and the 18th page in Macedonian on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor, Article 25 of this rule book says that: "In relation to reviewing specific matters, preparations of draft regulations, giving opinions and proposals for specific matters, as well as conducting specific duties within the competencies of the ministry, permanent or temporary professional commissions and working groups can be formed." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. In the Macedonian text, it states: "To [Macedonian spoken] "proucuvanje," which should be translated more as "studying."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Who in the ministry has the authority to establish these commissions?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commissions of this type in the ministry can be set up by all those who head various organisational units in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So we've got persons who head organisational units in the ministry; and in this case, we've seen a number of decisions where the minister, himself, established commissions to look into different matters. So would it be fair to say that the minister has also the authority to set up commissions?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In cases where the law has authorised him to do so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, are there particular provisions and particular laws that authorise a minister of the interior to set up a particular kind of commission?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And which law or laws are those?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, he establishes the members of disciplinary commissions. For example, he determines the membership of the commissions who provide licences to companies which carry out driving exams.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is there a specific law or legal provision that says the minister has the authority to set up a commission to examine the conduct of the members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs in a particular village at a particular time?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with the Law on Government, the government [as interpreted] can set up such a commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, sorry, that wasn't my question. I'll repeat --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It was my -- I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, where in the rule book does it say that the minister has the right or the prerogative to establish commissions? It doesn't say that in Article 25, does it?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 25 is a general provision, which enables commissions to be set up whenever that is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor Taseva, isn't this rule book lex specialis to the broader laws of the government of Macedonia, including the Law on Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This rule book enables commissions to be set up at all times when a certain effort has to be done which is a task.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. I'm very sorry. I want you to answer the question that I just asked you, a very simple straightforward question. I'll ask it again. Isn't this rule book lex specialis to the law on government, the laws of the government of Macedonia, including the Law on Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This rule book is not a lex specialis. It just regulates the manner of carrying out concern powers of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Based on -- and those powers given to the Ministry of Interior are paws provided by the general laws and the constitution of the Republic of Macedonia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are also other by-laws in addition to this rule book. This is why it can be considered as an only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So this rule book, then, would be lex specialis to the Law on Internal Affairs, the constitution, and other laws of the Republic of Macedonia that describe the powers of persons who work for the Ministry of Internal Affairs, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It explains in more concrete terms the manner in which matters and work related to internal affairs should be carried out. And it does not go to the full end it because there are also other acts which further explain provisions within this rule book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can I take your last response, then, as a "yes" to my question?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It explains part of the competencies, not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So there are issues that are explained in other by-laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. I'm glad we've gotten there now. So if this rule book is lexis specialis, then Article 25 should refer to specific persons in the Ministry of Internal Affairs who have the authority to set up commissions. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not like that, since this is a broad provision that leaves room to establish various types of committees within various bodies on various levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Tell me, Professor, where in the laws of Republic of Macedonia or the Law on Internal Affairs does it say that the minister of internal affairs can set up a commission to investigate the conduct of members of the ministry in a particular village? Where is that expressly stated in the law?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is not stated expressly in the law. The law only states that commissions could be established of various types, depending on the needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And over the years, different ministers of the interior have assumed the authority, haven't they, for establishing such commissions, right? They have assumed that authority for themselves, haven't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, since such committees were established many times also by other heads at various levels within the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But if there's no specific law that says a minister can set up this kind of commission, or these kinds of commissions, then this kind of authority is something that, over time, ministers have taken for themselves, in addition to the fact that other heads of other parts of the ministry could also set up these commissions. Right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not right, since the heads of bodies can also establish commissions, such as, for instance, the commission established in cooperation with the local self-government and the schools. To overcome the problem with the juvenile crime or use of drugs, such commissions can be established by individuals who are working at the local level. So depending on the need, the commission is established.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to move on now, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to, in the English translation, the next page, and if we could focus on Article 26. It's on the same page in the Macedonian version. And I think there is a small probably typographical error in the first line of Article 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could focus on this with me, Professor Taseva, Article 26, the first line says: "A collegium exists within the ministry acting as an advisory body for the minister." Is that what it says in the Macedonian original as well?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. So, if I understand correctly, the members of the collegium give advice to the minister on different issues, and then the minister makes decisions, based on the advice that he receives. Is that how it works?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what is written here. I said that I have never been a member of the collegium, so I can't speak from my own experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But, as an expert, that is your understanding how this works, how the system works?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yes, this is what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Professor, the members of the collegium would be the, to use your term, the professional members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs that you mentioned in your direct examination, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I did not follow you because I was reading again the Article 26 to see about those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor Taseva, during your direct examination, you -- you made a distinction between the minister as someone with a political function and his close colleagues in the ministry, the directors for example, you described them as professionals. My question is simply this: The members of the collegium, apart from the minister, would be the professional members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs that you mentioned previously, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the deputy minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. You see, during your direct examination, you told my colleague, Ms. Residovic, or you agreed with a proposition put to you by Ms. Residovic, that it is the professionals in the Ministry of Internal Affairs who have the last word in the work of the ministry. I don't understand, Professor, how both things could be correct, because you've told us today that the members of the collegium, which include these what you call the professionals, they give advice to the minister, and the minister makes decisions based on that advice. So why did you tell my colleague previously that it's the professionals who have the last word?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decisions that the minister brings are political decisions. The decisions that pertain to the performance of duty of the Ministry of Interior are something that is carried out by professionals exclusively, and the decisions are made by the professionals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Isn't your testimony, Professor Taseva -- let's think back to 2001 now. That was a difficult time. Ljube Boskoski was the minister of internal affairs. People were being killed. People were displaced from their homes. Is it your testimony that Minister Boskoski would not have made a single decision related to the performance of the duty or the work of members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs? Is that your evidence? I just want to understand you.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decisions are brought at the level of collegium, and the minister discusses all the decisions with the collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the minister then, if there is the -- the minister is going to make the decision, isn't he, on an important issue. That's why they have collegiums, to discuss them, so the minister can be informed. Right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so that the minister is informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, as you said, the decisions are brought at the level of collegium, the minister discusses them with the collegium, and then the minister will make a final decision. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When authorised by the law to pass a decision, the minister will pass a decision. That decision could be also to request information that they will send to the government. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For example -- I'm sorry. I interrupted you. Well, for example, we looked at Article 10 of the Law on Internal Affairs a few minutes ago, which was -- that was P86, Exhibit P86. A second part of Article 10 gives the minister powers to order authorised officials to perform "certain activities at a time when the public peace and order is deranged." So, for example, back in 2001, would it be possible that the minister might have made some decisions to use his powers to instruct certain authorised officials to conduct certain activities? Isn't that possible?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decisions were brought at the level of Ministry of Interior. I could not give you offhand assessments or speculate on how were the decisions made and who brought those decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor, you've come here to testify as an expert on how the Ministry of Internal Affairs functioned in 2001. Are you saying you're not -- you're not able to tell us or you're not able to answer my question as to what the minister might have done back in 2001, pursuant to Article 10?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't, because I'm not a direct participant in those events you are looking for a direct answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor, your report talks about, for example, joint operations. You told us earlier you never participated in a joint operation, but you've given us a piece of your expert about that, well footnoted. Your report talks about the mobilisation of reservists, even the demobilisation of reservists. I don't think you have ever been a police reserve; I could be wrong. Your report talks about criminal investigations; although, I stand corrected, you have participate in the criminal investigations. Your report talks about the interpretation of the amnesty law. I could be wrong, but I don't know whether you have been directly involved in matters related to prosecution or not related to the Law on Amnesty. Why are you telling us now that you can't give an opinion on something because you were not directly present or involved?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The questions that you -- or issues that you indicated now and which I speak about in my report are something that I had the opportunity to study and analyse when preparing my report; analysing laws, by-laws but also document atlas that pertain to those specific issues that I advanced my opinion. With regard to some of the issues and most part of the them, I also speak from my own personal experience. This specific question, the work of the minister's collegium, is something that I haven't studied and I can't give you a more specific answer on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You did look at the rule book for operations of the Ministry of Internal Affairs as part of the preparation of your report, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, in your report, you have an entire chapter, Chapter 5, called: The role and of the minister in the Ministry of Interior, paragraphs 56 to 69, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So why are you telling us now that you just can't say anything about the collegium, given the fact that it's even discussed in the materials that you reviewed for your report?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Working on my report and studying the documents that I reviewed when preparing my report, I was not looking for specific references to the way in which the minister's collegium operates, and I did not review that issue specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Would you agree, though, that the manner in which the minister's collegium operates would be relevant to the issue of how the Ministry of Internal Affairs operates. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And would you agree that the manner in which the minister's collegium operates would be relevant to the exercise of the powers and authorities of the minister. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this would need to be placed in correlation with the work of other substitutions such as the government when we're speaking specifically about the competencies of the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to move on briefly to another topic. Can you turn to paragraph 60, please, of your report. This is in the subchapter entitled, Delegated nature of responsibilities of the minister. Professor Taseva, paragraph 60 reads like this: "The law not only gives powers to the minister to do certain things. It also restricts his powers. In other words, the law authorises him to do certain things, and he is only allowed to undertake tasks and duties which the law authorises him to undertake." Have you been following me?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You don't cite any authority for the points that you make in that paragraph. Can you just tell me, briefly, on what did you rely to make these conclusions?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All laws mentioned at the beginning of this report and other laws that were not mentioned but which I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then why on such an important point in your report, Professor, didn't you mention, didn't you cite to any of these laws in the report, paragraph 60?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this is a general conclusion, and the specific provisions are found elsewhere in the report and in other references contained in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I see. Can you just tell us, please, point me, please, to the specific legal provisions that support what you say in paragraph 60, particularly the last sentence of paragraph 60.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are provisions also in the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Which provisions?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say from the top of my head. I need to see the law and I will indicate which ones they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see the time, Your Honour. Shall we take the first break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If that's convenient, Mr. Saxon. We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor Taseva, before the break, we were talking about paragraph 60 in your report, and, in particular, the last sentence which says: "In other words, the law authorises him," the minister, "to do certain things and he is only allowed to undertake tasks and duties which the law authorises him to undertake." You told us that authority for this proposition would be found in the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So if we can show the witness now what is Exhibit P86, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you could direct us, please, Professor, to the provisions of this law that support what you say in paragraph 60.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I presented in item 60 of my report is a general observation about the legal positioning of the position minister. I said this at the end of the previous session, that what the law provides for the minister is also incorporated in the Law on Internal Affairs; that is to say, it is not only this law as we were able to see previously the Law on Organisation of the Government and the Law on Organisation of State as administration, including also the Law on Internal Affairs as well as other laws provide powers to the minister as to -- as to what he can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor Taseva, I'm going to stop you there, please. Before the break, I asked you this question: "Can you just tell us, please, point me, please, to the specific legal provisions that support what you say in paragraph 60, particularly the last sentence of paragraph 60." You answered: "These are provisions also in the Law on Internal Affairs." I asked you: "Which provisions?" You said: "I couldn't say from the top of my head. I need to see the law and I will indicate which ones they are." So can you point, please, to a single provision in the Law on Internal Affairs that supports what you say in the last sentence to paragraph 60 of your report.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is essential, I would ask that I receive a hard copy of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could the usher please provide the witness with my binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Here we have a hard copy of the text in English and Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one such example is Article 11 of the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn in e-court to Article 11, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor, how does Article 11 stand for the proposition that you make in paragraph 60 or support the proposition that you make in paragraph 60: "In other words, the law authorises him to do certain things and he is only allowed to undertake tasks and duties which the law authorises him to undertake." How does Article 11 support that proposition?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 11 provides specifically a power to the minister. The law authorises the minister to undertake certain activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is that your response?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How does Article 11 support the proposition that: "He is only allowed to undertake tasks and duties which the law authorises him to undertake"? How does Article 11 support that proposition?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This sentence from my report is supported in many other laws, has its support in many other laws, in all laws that establish --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there. Sorry to interrupt. I would like you to answer the question that I asked you: How does Article 11 support the proposition that the minister is only allowed to undertake tasks and duties which the law authorises him to undertake?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister has the authority to undertake that which is provided by law as his competency, and these are the competencies of the minister and this is what he is allowed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How does Article 11 in any way support the proposition that the minister is only allowed to undertake tasks and duties which the law authorises him to undertake?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My observation and position in this report is the result of the review and analysis of everything that pertains to the competency of a minister, including, and specifically in this case, the minister of the interior. What is given to him as authority by the law is that which the minister can undertake.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that is your interpretation of the law, isn't it? That's how your reading all these laws, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is my interpretation of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor, doesn't the rather narrow interpretation of the powers available to the minister of the interior, which you express in paragraph 60 of your report, conflict with the principle of interpretation used to describe the president's powers over joint operations in paragraph 17 of your report?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you turn to paragraph 17, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: See, in the last sentence in paragraph 17, you say: "Nothing in the constitution or any other law would prevent the president, himself, to command or direct a joint operation." So you appear to be suggesting here that, well, if the law doesn't expressly prevent something, then the president can do it. Why, then, why do you record that interpretive model for the powers given to the president in a more restrictive interpretive framework for the powers accorded to the minister?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my way of thinking, both positions in my report are fully consistent, because this also falls within the same manner of interpretation of the legal provisions correct -- correctly and precisely what is written in the laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, you see, in paragraph 17, you seem to be interpreting the constitution and the laws to be saying, well, if the constitution and the laws don't prohibit an activity, then the president can do it. But in paragraph 60, you say that the minister can only do things, can only undertake tasks and duties which the law authorises him to undertake. So, in other words, if it is not in the law, he can't do it. You don't see a contradiction there?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see a contradiction. Also, I don't see anywhere in my report the word "prohibition." I'm speaking in general terms that with my analysis of the laws and other documents, I have concluded that nothing in the laws would prevent or limit the president to practice his constitutional powers, while many laws contain provisions which clearly establish which activities a minister can undertake and what are the powers of a minister and specifically the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, if there's nothing in the law that would prevent or limit a minister of the interior, say, from organising a birthday party for a family member at his office, by the same token, then, then the minister could undertake that activity, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. This is so, and I can organise this event, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so, for example, in a period of crisis, if there's nothing in the law that expressly prevent or limit the minister of the interior, say, from sending a group of authorised officials to conduct a particular activity, or sending an authorised official to conduct a particular activity, then the minister can do that, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For this type of activities, the professional structures of the ministry are competent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question. My question is: If, during a crisis time, if there's nothing in the law that expressly prevents or limits a minister from directing an authorised official to conduct a particular activity, then the minister can do that, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He cannot, because this is not within his competency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If there's nothing in a particular law that expressly prohibits it, then, on the same principle that we've been discussing, the minister should be able to do it, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The laws clearly establish the authorisations of the minister. This is not enumerated as a competency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Article 10 of the Law on Internal Affairs says that in times when public peace and order is seriously deranged, the minister can order an authorised official or officials to carry out certain activities. So, if, during the crisis time, the minister wanted to authorise an authorised official to carry out a certain activity, if that activity is not expressly prohibited in the law, then the minister could do it, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister can order what is written down specifically in the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what if there's some room for interpretation in what is written down in the law, like the phrase "certain activities"?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister cannot undertake activities which are outside his competencies. Previously I also said that in our legal definition of public peace and order, or public law and order, cases are specifically defined which signify a disruption of public law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Professor, do you suppose that fighting between two groups, fighting between members of the security forces of the Republic of Macedonia and another group calling themselves the NLA that involves the use of automatic rifles, rocket-propelled grenades, tanks, artillery, helicopters, fixed-wing aircraft, you don't think that would qualify as a disruption of public peace and order?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see. And so, for example, if such activities occurred in 2001, if I understand you then, for example, rather than exercising his powers accorded to him under Article 10 of the Law on Internal Affairs, the minister would just do nothing, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ministry and other state bodies can undertake measures, but this measure does not fall within the measures taken in situations such as these. These are measures foreseen for a situation when the public peace and order is disturbed; for example, demonstrations; for example, clashes between reporters of two teams and other such examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How about clashes between members of two different ethnic communities? Would that qualify as a disturbance of the public law and order?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the type of clashes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean that if they are -- if they meet on the street or in front of the parliament building, which does happen, this means disturbance of the public law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, what if they meet in a more rural area? What if they meet in a village somewhere? Isn't that disturbance of the public law and order?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it would depend on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So it might --

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they're having an argument in the village pub, then we have a case of disturbance of public law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. You said, in your direct examination, that the minister of internal affairs does not perform operative tasks operation or operations within the areas of work provided in the Law on Internal Affairs. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But the minister, to be an efficient an effective minister, must supervise how those operations and operative tasks are carried out. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And, for example, if the minister doesn't like the way certain operative employees are doing their job, the minister might tell them to do it differently, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister can speak with them why they're acting in the way they are, but he cannot tell them how they should act.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, the minister could tell the director of public security to tell the operative employees to act differently, can't he?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The director for the directorate of public security acts independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, suppose the minister is not happy with the performance of the director? Is the minister simply supposed to stand by and remain silent and do nothing, while operative activities are carried out in an unsatisfactory fashion?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the minister has a problem with the work of the director, then he should inform the government of this, the government who appointed the director, and to ask that specific measures be taken, whether this will be removal of the director or perhaps other measures which the government can undertake.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you say that because the minister, he can propose -- he can propose who should be appointed as director by the government, and the minister also proposes -- can make a proposal to have a director dismissed by the government. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The government appoints the director.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the government does that upon a proposal of the minister, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government appoints the director independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Taseva, are you telling the Chamber that the government does not -- that, in practice, the government does not appoint the director of public security upon a proposal of the minister of the interior? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we see now the legal provisions related to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, Ms. Taseva. You're the expert. You're supposed to know about this. You've testified at length about the public security bureau and the director. Can you answer my question?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government appoints the director of the bureau for public security independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the government will appoint that director upon a proposal of the minister, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness what is 65 ter -- this is a video-clip. It will be played in Sanction. It's 65 ter 1117.6, ERN V000-4741 -- it's V000-7471, and it is a video made on the 29th of July, 2002, in Tetovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like you to watch the video, please, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Stop there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask my learned friend, before he asks the question, could he just clarify for us when was this speech made and what was the occasion for it. Is this the minister's speech, or is it something completely different? I'm asking this because of the words heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It is a speech by then-Minister Boskoski at or during a political campaign on the 29th of July, 2002 in the city of Tetovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask you to say also what was the political campaign. Was it the general elections or a political --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It is my understanding that this was part of the political campaign of the accused and other members of his party for the general elections that occurred later in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Professor, in your opinion, can the minister of the interior lawfully take part in political campaigns, in electoral campaigns?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All ministers in the Republic of Macedonia participate in political campaigns.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And where is this authorisation or ability codified in the constitution or the laws; do you know?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that the constitution or laws provide such approval or authorisations to participate in election campaigns.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, maybe I can help you a little bit with the constitution of Macedonia, Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours this is Exhibit P00091.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For example, Article 16 subparagraph 2 refers to the freedom of speech; although, it doesn't specifically refer to election campaigns. Article 20, subparagraph 1, refers to freedom of association to exercise political and other rights; although, it doesn't explicitly to electoral campaigns or to ministers. But would it be fair to say that implicit in these provisions of the constitution or these provisions of the constitution could be interpreted to give ministers the ability or the authority to take part in political campaigns while they are ministers? Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This constitutional provision belongs to the chapter of provisions on basic human rights and freedoms, and then they give the right to every citizen of the Republic of Macedonia to participate in such type of activities: Freedom of speech, freedom of organisation and meeting, of associating. The laws contain restrictions with regards to the professional part of the state administration, and the bodies of state administration, with regards to their ability or eligibility to participate in campaigns. I spoke about the professional part, while the minister and all ministers belong to political part of the administration and there are no provisions that would restrict their participation in such type of activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And since there are no provisions in the laws that restrict ministers from taking part in these political activities, then that means that ministers are able to take part in these activities, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ministers are politicians and they are members of political parties who participate in exercise of power after the elections were won, and the understanding of politics in the Republic of Macedonia is such that all political office holders participate in the political activities. Whether those are campaigns or other types of activities, that is not always relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. So another way of looking at what a minister can or cannot do would be to, for example, look at the understanding of politics in the Republic of Macedonia, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said previously that what the minister can do or cannot do is precisely stipulated in the laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, all right. But let's go back to my question which you haven't really answered. Since there are no provisions in the laws that restrict ministers from taking part in these political activities, then that means that ministers are able to take part in these activities. That's right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Da [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The witness said "da," but we did not hear anything.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to a different topic, Professor Taseva. During your direct examination, Ms. Residovic asked you to confirm whether: "The directors of the bodies within the ministry are independent in the performance of their tasks and the minister could not exert influence over those bodies to prevent them from lawfully performing their duties." You answered: "Yes. This is the legal provision. This is the legal position." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And my question for you is: Back in 2001, could the minister exert influence over the director of public security and the bodies of the ministry to -- to ensure that they lawfully perform their duties?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister can monitor their work through the bodies in the ministry, such as the collegium, but the minister could not impose or exert his influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, again, if the minister doesn't like how the director of public security is carrying out one aspect of his work, particularly in a time of crisis, wouldn't the minister logically tell the director of public security, how the minister feels and tell the director to change his performance?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could not order the director anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the directors are independent, autonomous, in the performance of their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what is the purpose of having a minister then?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister is the political manager and head of the ministry that he is in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. And as the manager and head of the ministry, the minister is responsible for what -- the acts and conduct of the employees of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, right?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He is competent to carry out tasks from within the competency of that ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so how can the minister carry out his responsibilities if he can't tell the director what to do in a given situation?

utterances.speaker: SLAGJANA TASEVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister of the interior cannot issue orders to other structures within the ministry. This is why the other bodies are structured and established, such as the collegium, and the law provides that there are two independent bodies within the ministry that perform their duties autonomously. The minister can coordinate, can convene collegiums when certain issues would be discussed, but the minister cannot order in which way to act.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
